facts.claim: "The Alcott" is the seventh track on The National's ninth studio album, First Two Pages of Frankenstein, released April 28, 2023 on 4AD.
The song is credited to three writers: Matt Berninger, Aaron Dessner and Taylor Swift.
The National produced the track at Long Pond studio in the Hudson Valley, New York.
Aaron Dessner first wrote the music. Berninger wrote the main part of the song to it, and Dessner sent it to Swift, who he knew liked the music.
Swift replied with a voice memo containing all her parts, with lyrics she had added in dialogue with Berninger.
Berninger says he wrote the song with his wife Carin in mind. Swift added her own perspective and wrote all of her parts.
Berninger told Variety that Swift wrote a whole different perspective onto a song he had written about his wife, so the song suddenly had two sides.
Berninger said he imagined a contained moment and narrative between two people. The song is set to sparse piano and strings, with a couple trying to revive a troubled relationship.
It is Swift's second duet with The National's Berninger, after "Coney Island" on evermore. Aaron Dessner co-produced Swift's 2020 albums Folklore and evermore.
The National formed in Brooklyn in 1999 and are friends from Cincinnati. The lineup is Matt Berninger, brothers Aaron and Bryce Dessner, and brothers Scott and Bryan Devendorf.

research.lineage: The song sits in The National's brooding, piano-led indie rock tradition, and it extends the Aaron Dessner–Taylor Swift folk-leaning collaborations that began with Folklore and evermore.

draft:
Someone is sitting in the corner in the back of a place called **The Alcott**, writing in a golden notebook about "someone / Who used to be me." The narrator walks in already knowing this. That's the setup Matt Berninger built, a single contained scene between two people. He has said he wrote it with his wife, Carin, in mind. Then Taylor Swift answered it, and the song stopped being one man's confession and became an argument with two sides.

The music came first. Aaron Dessner wrote it and Berninger wrote the main body of the song over it. Dessner sent it to Swift, who sent back a voice memo with all her parts, lyrics she wrote in dialogue with Berninger. It's their second duet after "Coney Island," and it extends the partnership Dessner and Swift started on Folklore and evermore. The National produced it at Long Pond in the Hudson Valley.

The arrangement stays out of the way. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar circles under a slow, sustained bass line. Unhurried drums lean on the snare, and a synth pad hangs in a big, clean room. Berninger sings low and breathy, close to the mic, like he's talking across a small table. Then a second, higher voice slides in beside him in close harmony, and the blend is so smooth it almost hides how much the two of them disagree.

The disagreement is the song. Berninger's narrator knows exactly what he's doing. He waits for her to look up, sees her smile, and then wonders how many times he can pull this before she stops believing him. The pride of still being wanted sits right next to the shame of using it. The chorus swaps its pronouns as it goes, so the reluctance passes from one of them to the other. By the end, the narrator is admitting he never wanted to fall back in either.

Swift's counter-lines crowd in around that chorus and won't let it settle. "Have I become one of your problems?" turns his confession back on him. Then comes the line that keeps the song from being a simple apology: "'Cause I love this curse on our house." Neither of them wants out. Berninger's long run of "I'll ruin it all over" isn't a threat or a plea. It's a forecast, and the second voice answers it with something close to an invitation.

Nothing gets fixed. The song closes on the same three words it keeps returning to, back in love, and that's the point. What sticks is the sound of two people who can each see the wreck coming, and who reach for each other anyway because the wreck is theirs.
